421.title: Fret not (Psalm 37)
421.hook: don't fret because of evildoers; delight in the Lord
421.howItsDone: Christians turn to Psalm 37 when struggling with envy or injustice, and its line 'the meek shall inherit the earth' is often read alongside the Beatitudes in Matthew 5.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Psalm thirty-four: taste first, then see. Your line was taste and see. Did you eat one bite slowly? Day four hundred twenty-one.

The coworker who cuts corners gets the promotion. The neighbor who never returns anything just bought a boat. The person who was cruel to you in school seems to be thriving, at least online. You've done things the honest way, and it hasn't paid off, and they've done it the other way, and it has. So you stew. You replay it in the shower. You check their profile one more time, and feel worse. If that sounds familiar, there's a whole psalm for it. And it opens with two words that sound old-fashioned, but describe that feeling exactly.
screen: `THE CORNER-CUTTER GETS PROMOTED.` → `YOU STEW IN THE SHOWER.` → `TWO OLD-FASHIONED WORDS.`

segments.voice: Psalm thirty-seven, in the King James Bible: "Fret not thyself because of evildoers, neither be thou envious against the workers of iniquity." Fret, in Hebrew, comes from a word that means to burn, to get heated. Don't heat yourself up. Notice the word thyself. Fretting is something you do to you. The person who cheated is out on their boat, and you're the one who's burning. The psalm says they're like grass, which withers quickly. Their success, the psalm says, is real, but it's short. Then instead of fretting, three verbs. Trust: trust in the LORD, and do good. Delight: "Delight thyself also in the LORD; and he shall give thee the desires of thine heart." Not, you'll get whatever you want. More like, delight in God, and your desires themselves begin to change. And rest: "Rest in the LORD, and wait patiently for him: fret not thyself because of him who prospereth in his way." Fret not appears three times in the first eight verses, as if the writer knows you'll need to hear it more than once. Then comes a line people sometimes don't realize is from the Psalms: "But the meek shall inherit the earth; and shall delight themselves in the abundance of peace." Jesus echoes it in the Sermon on the Mount: blessed are the meek. And near the end, an old man speaks: "I have been young, and now am old." It's a wisdom psalm, more like advice from a grandparent than a prayer. Not everyone's experience matches every line, and the Bible itself has other books, like Job, that wrestle with when the righteous do suffer. But this psalm's counsel is steady: don't let someone else's wrongdoing set you on fire.
screen: `FRET: DON'T HEAT YOURSELF UP.` · `TRUST, DELIGHT, REST.` · `THE MEEK SHALL INHERIT THE EARTH.` · `I HAVE BEEN YOUNG, AND NOW AM OLD.` · then, large: `FRET NOT THYSELF BECAUSE OF EVILDOERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let go of one grudge. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone whose success, or whose getting away with something, keeps you heated. Notice where the heat sits in your body: jaw, chest, stomach. You don't have to pretend they were right. You don't have to stop wanting justice. Just notice that you're the one burning. On each out-breath, let a little of the heat go. Trust. Delight. Rest. If you pray, you can hand the person, and the justice, to God. If not, simply set the grudge down for this minute. The bell holds the time.
Fret not. Psalm thirty-seven's advice when the wrong people seem to win: don't heat yourself up. Trust, delight, and rest instead.
Your line: fret not. Today, the next time you start replaying what someone else got away with, stop, and say the two words to yourself. Day four hundred twenty-one.

422.title: As the deer (Psalm 42)
422.hook: as a deer pants for water; why are you cast down, my soul?
422.carry: why so cast down, my soul?
422.howItsDone: Many Christians turn to Psalm 42 in seasons of spiritual dryness, grief or homesickness; it is chanted in monastic daily prayer and sung in hymn versions such as "As pants the hart for cooling streams."

segments.voice: Yesterday, Psalm thirty-seven, for anyone lying awake replaying what someone else got away with. Your line was fret not. Did you set one grudge down, even for an hour? Day four hundred twenty-two.

The stream bed is mostly stones now. A deer comes down the hillside the way it always has, to the place where the water ran in spring, and stands there, sides heaving, nose low, searching. It knows exactly what it needs. It just can't find enough of it. Now set a person beside that deer. Someone who used to walk at the front of the crowd on feast days, singing all the way up to the house of God, and who now lives far away, while the people around him ask, again and again, so where's your God now? Today's psalm opens with that deer. And then it does something unusual. The writer turns around and starts talking to his own soul.
screen: `A DRY STREAM BED.` → `A THIRSTY DEER.` → `A HOMESICK SINGER.`

segments.voice: Psalm forty-two begins, in the King James Bible: "As the hart panteth after the water brooks, so panteth my soul after thee, O God." A hart is an old English word for a male deer. The Hebrew for those brooks means channels of water, the kind that run full in the rainy season and can shrink to nothing in a dry one, so many readers picture an animal hunting for water that's hard to find. That is the feeling of the whole psalm. Its heading gives it to the sons of Korah, a family of temple singers. The writer remembers leading the crowds to the house of God with shouts of joy. Now he's far off, by the Jordan and the slopes of Mount Hermon, and he says: "My tears have been my meat day and night, while they continually say unto me, Where is thy God?" Meat, in older English, simply meant food. He has been living on tears. Then comes the turn that makes this psalm so human. He speaks to himself. "Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted in me? hope thou in God." He asks his own sadness a question, and then gives it a gentle instruction. Not snap out of it. Hope. The same lines come back three times, twice here and once in Psalm forty-three, which is one reason many scholars think the two psalms began as a single poem. And between the refrains, the sadness doesn't vanish: "Deep calleth unto deep," he says, every wave going over his head. In this psalm, thirst isn't a failure of faith. It's a measure of how much someone wants God.
screen: `A HART AT THE WATER BROOKS` · `TEARS FOR FOOD, DAY AND NIGHT` · `WHY ART THOU CAST DOWN, O MY SOUL?` · `THIRST IS A MEASURE OF WANTING` · then, large: `HOPE THOU IN GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: speak kindly to your own soul. Sit, and let your breathing slow. Notice what is low in you today. Tiredness, a worry, missing someone, a place you can't get back to. Don't push it away. Ask it the psalm's question, quietly, the way you'd ask a friend who looked down: why so cast down? Then listen. Whatever comes, answer it gently, without a lecture. If you pray, you can add the psalm's own words: hope thou in God. If you don't, just keep your soul company for a while. The bell holds the time.
As the deer. The opening of Psalm forty-two: a thirsty animal searching for water, and a person who misses God that much.
Your line: why so cast down, my soul? Today, when you hear yourself talking harshly to yourself, swap the lecture for the question. Ask it gently, and wait for an answer. Day four hundred twenty-two.

423.title: A very present help (Psalm 46)
423.hook: though the mountains shake into the sea, God is our refuge
423.tomorrow: create in me a clean heart
423.howItsDone: Christians often pray Psalm 46 in times of disaster, war or fear, and it lies behind Martin Luther's hymn "A Mighty Fortress Is Our God," still sung in many churches.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a deer at the water brooks and a singer talking to his own soul. Your line was why so cast down, my soul? Did you ask it gently, and wait for an answer? Day four hundred twenty-three.

Most phones have a place for an emergency contact. One name, one number, for the moment something goes badly wrong and someone else has to make the call. People don't usually pick the most impressive person they know. They pick the one who picks up. The one who has shown up before, at two in the morning, at the hospital, on moving day. Psalm forty-six is a song about that kind of help. Months ago on this path we met its most famous verse, be still. Today, the rest of the song: the earthquake that comes before the stillness, and a river that, on any map of Jerusalem, shouldn't be there.
screen: `AN EMERGENCY CONTACT.` → `THE ONE WHO PICKS UP.` → `A RIVER THAT SHOULDN'T BE THERE.`

segments.voice: The psalm opens, in the King James Bible: "God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble." In 1611, very present meant near at hand, right there. The Hebrew says it a little differently: a help in troubles, found very much. Found again and again. Help with a track record. Then the song gets loud. "Therefore will not we fear, though the earth be removed, and though the mountains be carried into the midst of the sea." Waters roar, mountains shake, nations rage. Nothing in this psalm pretends trouble isn't real. And right in the middle of the noise, verse four: "There is a river, the streams whereof shall make glad the city of God." Here's the surprise. Jerusalem had no river. It had a spring, the Gihon, and water carried through tunnels, but no river running through its streets. So the psalm sings one anyway. Outside, the sea roars and swallows mountains. Inside, a quiet river makes a city glad. Many readers hear it as a picture of God's presence in the middle of his people. Then verse five: God will help her, "and that right early." In the Hebrew, that's at the turning of the morning. The help arrives as the night ends. Twice the psalm repeats its chorus: "The LORD of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our refuge." And each time, one more word: Selah. Nobody knows for sure what it means. Many think it marked a pause in the music. Which may be the best place to put it. Right after the line about who's with us.
screen: `HELP FOUND, AGAIN AND AGAIN` · `MOUNTAINS CARRIED INTO THE SEA` · `A RIVER IN A CITY WITHOUT ONE` · `HELP AT THE TURNING OF MORNING` · then, large: `THE LORD OF HOSTS IS WITH US.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: breathe through one anxious moment. Sit, and bring to mind one thing that has been making your chest tight. Let it be there, like the roaring water in the psalm. Don't fight it and don't solve it. Then look for the river. Breathe in slowly, and let the breath out longer than it came in. Again. Feel where your body is held up: the chair, the floor. If you pray, you can say the first verse once, slowly: God is our refuge and strength. If you don't, just keep breathing, long and slow, until the bell. The bell holds the time.
A very present help. Psalm forty-six's name for God: help that is near, and has been found, again and again, in trouble.
Your line: a very present help. Today, when anxiety rises, take three slow breaths before anything else, and then notice who or what is actually near you. Day four hundred twenty-three.

424.title: Create in me a clean heart (Psalm 51)
424.word: Create in me a clean heart
424.hook: David's prayer after his great wrong: a broken heart you won't despise
424.howItsDone: Psalm 51 is one of the Church's great prayers of repentance: Catholics, Orthodox, Anglicans and Lutherans pray it in Lent and on Ash Wednesday, and many Christians pray verse 10 before confession or at the start of the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a river in a city that had none. Your line was a very present help. When something shook you, what was actually near? Day four hundred twenty-four.

The prophet Nathan walks into the palace with a story. Two men in one town. One rich, with flocks and herds. One poor, with a single little ewe lamb he raised with his own children, that ate from his plate and slept in his arms. A guest arrives at the rich man's house, and instead of taking from his own flocks, the rich man takes the poor man's lamb and serves it for dinner. King David is furious. That man deserves to die, he says. And Nathan answers with four words: "Thou art the man." David has taken Bathsheba, another man's wife, and arranged for her husband Uriah to die in battle. The heading of today's psalm places it right here, in the silence after those four words.
screen: `ONE LITTLE EWE LAMB.` → `THOU ART THE MAN.` → `THE SILENCE AFTER.`

segments.voice: Psalm fifty-one begins, in the King James Bible: "Have mercy upon me, O God, according to thy lovingkindness." No excuses. No explaining why it was different. He asks to be washed, thoroughly, and cleansed. Then verse ten, the line many Christians know by heart: "Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me." Look at the verb. Create. In Hebrew it's bara, the same verb as the first line of the Bible, in the beginning God created. In its usual form, the Bible uses it only with God as the one doing it. So David isn't asking for a stain remover. He knows scrubbing won't be enough. He's asking God to do for his heart what God did for the world: make something new where there was only chaos. Then the psalm goes further. Sacrifices and offerings, he says, aren't what God is after. "The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise." Contrite means crushed, ground down. The thing you'd expect God to turn away from, the wreckage, is the one thing he won't refuse. Many scholars think the psalm headings were added later, and debate who wrote it; tradition has long heard it as David's own. Either way, churches made it their great prayer of turning around. In Latin it's called the Miserere, from its first word. Catholics, Orthodox, Anglicans and Lutherans pray it in Lent and on Ash Wednesday, and many begin each morning with its verse fifteen: O Lord, open thou my lips.
screen: `HAVE MERCY. NO EXCUSES.` · `CREATE: THE VERB OF GENESIS 1` · `NOT SCRUBBED. MADE NEW.` · `A BROKEN HEART, NOT DESPISED` · then, large: `CREATE IN ME A CLEAN HEART, O GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let yourself be still. Bring to mind one thing you wish you hadn't done. Not the whole list, just one. Don't argue the case for yourself, and don't pile on. Let it be what it was. If you pray, you can say verse ten slowly, a few times, letting the words land: create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me. If you don't pray, simply hold the wish for a fresh start, without forcing it. Breathe. The bell holds the time.
Create in me a clean heart. David's plea after Nathan's story, using the same Hebrew verb as the first line of Genesis: not a cleaning, a new creation.
screen: `CREATE IN ME A CLEAN HEART — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: a clean heart. Today, if you need to make something right, skip the explanation and start with the honest part. Day four hundred twenty-four.

425.title: My soul waits (Psalm 62)
425.hook: truly my soul waits upon God in silence
425.howItsDone: Many Christians practice silent prayer, sitting quietly before God without words; Quaker meetings for worship gather in shared silence, and monasteries keep set hours of quiet.

segments.voice: Yesterday, David after Nathan's story, asking not to be scrubbed but made new. Your line was a clean heart. Did you start somewhere with the honest part? Day four hundred twenty-five.

Most waiting is noisy. Hold music, the same eight bars on a loop. Refreshing the tracking page. Checking whether the message has been read yet. Scrolling while the kettle boils, because three minutes of nothing feels unbearable. We wait with our hands full and our heads louder than ever. Psalm sixty-two describes a different kind of waiting. No music, no scrolling, no rehearsing what you'll say. Its heading names Jeduthun, one of the musicians of the temple, and yet the psalm's opening line, in Hebrew, is about silence. Today, the soul that waits without filling the gap.
screen: `HOLD MUSIC. REFRESH. REFRESH.` → `THREE MINUTES FEELS UNBEARABLE.` → `A QUIETER KIND OF WAITING.`

segments.voice: The King James Bible opens the psalm this way: "Truly my soul waiteth upon God: from him cometh my salvation." The Hebrew is stranger and more beautiful. Read word for word, it says something like: only toward God, my soul is silence. The word is dumiyyah, a hush, a stillness. Not a soul that's busy waiting. A soul that has gone quiet in God's direction. Then verse two: "He only is my rock and my salvation; he is my defence; I shall not be greatly moved." Greatly moved. He's honest. He expects to be shaken a little. Now listen to how the psalm repeats itself. Verse five tells his own soul, "wait thou only upon God; for my expectation is from him." And verse six repeats verse two almost exactly, except one word has gone missing. Greatly. Now it's simply, "I shall not be moved." Somewhere between the two verses, the silence has done its work. There's a small Hebrew word, ak, meaning only or truly, that turns up six times in this short psalm, like a hand tapping the same spot. Only God. Only the rock. And the silence isn't empty. Verse eight says, "pour out your heart before him." Quiet and honesty sit side by side. Christians have built whole ways of praying on this kind of quiet: monks keeping silence through the night, Quakers gathering in waiting worship, people in every church sitting in an empty sanctuary on a weekday. The psalm doesn't promise the wait will be short. It says what to wait toward.
screen: `ONLY TOWARD GOD, MY SOUL IS SILENCE` · `NOT GREATLY MOVED` · `FOUR VERSES LATER: NOT MOVED` · `QUIET, AND POUR OUT YOUR HEART` · then, large: `TRULY MY SOUL WAITETH UPON GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wait in silence for two minutes. Put the phone face down, out of reach. Sit, and let your hands rest. You're not waiting for anything to happen. You're just waiting toward. When thoughts come, and they will, let them pass like cars on a far road. If you pray, you can turn the silence toward God, with no words at all. If you don't, simply let the quiet be quiet. The bell holds the time.
My soul waits. Psalm sixty-two's opening: a soul that goes quiet toward God, and finds a rock to stand on.
Your line: in silence, waiting. Today, wait for one ordinary thing, a kettle, a page loading, a reply, without filling the gap. Let it be three minutes of nothing. Day four hundred twenty-five.

426.title: In a dry land (Psalm 63)
426.hook: my soul thirsts for you in a dry and weary land
426.howItsDone: Psalm 63 is a traditional morning psalm: Orthodox Christians read it among the six psalms at the start of Matins, and Catholics pray it at Sunday Morning Prayer in the Liturgy of the Hours.

segments.voice: Yesterday, my soul waits: a soul that goes quiet toward God. Your line was in silence, waiting. Did you let one small gap stay empty? Day four hundred twenty-six.

East of Jerusalem the land falls away fast. Within an hour's walk the green is gone, and the hills turn the color of bread crust, folding down toward the Dead Sea, one of the lowest places on earth. Shade is a rock's width. Water is a rumor. This is the wilderness of Judah, where shepherds have always known exactly how far it is to the next spring. The heading of Psalm sixty-three puts David here, on the run. Which time is a fair question. He fled into that wilderness from King Saul, and years later from his own son. Either way, a man with a crown or a claim to one is out in the dust, and his throat is dry.
screen: `EAST OF JERUSALEM.` → `THE WILDERNESS OF JUDAH.` → `A KING ON THE RUN.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible the psalm begins: "O God, thou art my God; early will I seek thee: my soul thirsteth for thee, my flesh longeth for thee in a dry and thirsty land, where no water is." Here's what the English hides. The Hebrew word for soul is nephesh. It means life, self, a living being. But it can also mean the throat, the neck, the place where breath and water go in. So when David says my soul thirsteth, a Hebrew listener could also hear: my throat is parched. The body and the longing are one word. He isn't using thirst as a pretty metaphor for a spiritual feeling. He is genuinely thirsty, and he notices that what he wants most is God. Then the psalm does something unexpected for a man in a desert. It praises. "Because thy lovingkindness is better than life, my lips shall praise thee." Better than life. Better than water, then, in a place where water is life. And it moves from dawn to night. "Early will I seek thee," it says at the start, and later, "When I remember thee upon my bed, and meditate on thee in the night watches." He lies awake in the dark, in a dry land, and remembers. Because of that word early, churches have prayed this psalm at the start of the day for many centuries. In the Orthodox morning service it's one of six psalms read in the half-dark, and in the Catholic Liturgy of the Hours it opens Sunday morning prayer. A desert psalm, prayed over coffee.
screen: `A DRY AND THIRSTY LAND` · `NEPHESH: SOUL, AND THROAT` · `BETTER THAN LIFE` · `A DESERT PSALM FOR EARLY MORNING` · then, large: `MY SOUL THIRSTETH FOR THEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: drink a glass of water slowly. If you can, pour one now. Hold it a moment. Notice the weight, the cold, the light in it. Take one small sip, and feel it all the way down your throat, the place the Hebrew calls nephesh. Then another. Don't hurry. Let your body tell you how much it wanted this. If you pray, you can let each sip carry the psalm's first words: O God, thou art my God. If you don't, just be thirsty, and be met. The bell holds the time.
In a dry land. Psalm sixty-three: David in the wilderness of Judah, with a dry throat and a soul thirsting for God.
Your line: thirsty for God. Today, every time you drink something, take the first sip slowly, and notice what else in you is thirsty. Day four hundred twenty-six.

427.title: How lovely (Psalm 84)
427.hook: even the sparrow finds a home near your altar; a day in your courts is better than a thousand
427.carry: even the sparrow has a home
427.tomorrow: teach us to number our days
427.howItsDone: Many Christians pray Psalm 84 when they arrive at church or go on pilgrimage, and it is sung in hymn settings and in Brahms's German Requiem as "How lovely are thy dwellings."

segments.voice: Yesterday, David in the dry land, and a word for soul that also means throat. Your line was thirsty for God. How did that first slow sip taste? Day four hundred twenty-seven.

Look up in an old train station, a barn, a covered market, and there's often a nest tucked on a beam where nobody can reach it. The building was made for trains or cows or fruit. The birds didn't ask. They just moved in, and nobody threw them out. Now go back nearly three thousand years, to the temple in Jerusalem. Pilgrims arrive dusty from the road. Priests move between the altars. Smoke rises. And up in the stonework, little birds are building nests and raising chicks, right next to the holiest place in the land. One pilgrim noticed, and envied them. Today, his song.
screen: `A NEST ON A STATION BEAM.` → `BIRDS IN THE TEMPLE.` → `A PILGRIM'S ENVY.`

segments.voice: Psalm eighty-four begins, in the King James Bible: "How amiable are thy tabernacles, O LORD of hosts!" In 1611, amiable meant lovely, lovable. The Hebrew word is close to beloved. This is a love song for a place. Then verse three: "Yea, the sparrow hath found an house, and the swallow a nest for herself, where she may lay her young, even thine altars." The Hebrew word for sparrow is a general word for any small bird. The point is how small. The least important creature in the courtyard gets to live where the pilgrim can only visit. Then the road. Those who travel to God's house, verse six says, pass through the valley of Baca, and make it a well. Nobody is sure what Baca means. It may be weeping, or a kind of tree that grows in dry places. Either way, the pilgrims turn a hard valley into springs as they walk through. And then the line people remember: "For a day in thy courts is better than a thousand. I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God, than to dwell in the tents of wickedness." Here's a detail worth knowing. The heading gives this psalm to the sons of Korah. Their ancestor Korah led a rebellion against Moses, and the book of Chronicles later lists Korah's descendants among the keepers of the gates. So the people singing that they'd rather stand at the door may have been the family whose job was the door. Brahms set this psalm in his German Requiem, and congregations still sing it as a hymn. A love song for being near.
screen: `AMIABLE: LOVELY, BELOVED` · `THE SMALLEST BIRD GETS A HOME` · `THE VALLEY BECOMES A SPRING` · `THE DOORKEEPERS SING IT` · then, large: `A DAY IN THY COURTS IS BETTER THAN A THOUSAND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit somewhere peaceful. It doesn't need to be a church. A bench, a window seat, the back step, a corner of your room with the light just right. Go there if you can, or picture it. Settle in like a bird on a beam. You don't have to earn the spot. Notice what makes this place feel like home: the light, the sound, the quiet. If you pray, you can whisper the psalm's first line: How amiable are thy tabernacles, O LORD of hosts. If you don't, simply rest where you are welcome. The bell holds the time.
How lovely. Psalm eighty-four's love song for God's house, where even a sparrow builds its nest by the altar.

Your line: even the sparrow has a home. That's a week in the Psalms: fret not, the thirsty deer, a very present help, a clean heart, a soul waiting in silence, a dry land, and today a nest by the altar. Today, make room for one small creature or one overlooked person. Day four hundred twenty-seven.
